idiom_name: (T, error) multiple return with early return, %w wrapping and errors.Is/errors.As
implementation_notes: Go's error contract is built into the language: fallible functions return a value and an error as two results, callers check err != nil first, and the failure is an ordinary interface value (error is predeclared; errors.New and fmt.Errorf construct it). Since Go 1.13 the reason travels structurally - %w wraps a cause, errors.Is compares against sentinels and errors.As extracts a concrete type - so callers branch on the failure without string matching, which is the Result pattern's error track realized with multiple return values instead of a wrapper type. What deliberately does not exist is the wrapper: re-encoding (T, error) into a generic Result[T] struct is unidiomatic. The `if err != nil { return ..., err }` early-return ladder replaces the combinator chain, verbose but explicit, and keeping error values small and defined at the layer that interprets them is the local discipline.
pitfalls: The error value can be ignored - Go has no must-use - so errcheck-style linters or review discipline are what stop `v, _ := f()` from silently dropping a failure.
Wrapping with %v instead of %w erases the chain and breaks errors.Is/errors.As on that path; wrap deliberately at every layer.
Sentinels compared with == only match when nothing wrapped them; use errors.Is for wrapped cases and errors.As when structured detail is needed.
